description_full: Canadian Pacific Kansas City Limited, together with its subsidiaries, owns and operates a transcontinental freight railway in Canada, the United States, and Mexico. The transports bulk commodities, including grain, coal, potash, fertilizers, and sulphur; merchandise freight consists of industrial and consumer products, such as forest products, energy, chemicals and plastics, metals, minerals, consumer products, and automotive; and intermodal traffic comprising retail goods in overseas containers. The company also provides rail and intermodal transportation services through a network of approximately 20,000 miles serving business centers. The company was formerly known as Canadian Pacific Railway Limited and changed its name to Canadian Pacific Kansas City Limited in April 2023. Canadian Pacific Kansas City Limited was founded in 1881 and is headquartered in Calgary, Canada.

Each employee generates $78K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 8× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: Canadian Pacific Kansas City Li is a large-cap industrials business with a $81.9B market cap on $10.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $1.5B in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.28× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.5×.

Shareholder yield of 4.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 28pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.34x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.67, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.13 vs 5y 0.62), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $182.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $62.65 (margin of safety -50%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $40.07 to $96.67 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 30.2 vs 24.1 and P/FCF 52.9 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 22% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $96.97 on average, 3% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.45).
It converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.28x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($129.0M of cash against $14.8B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.5x.
The current ratio of 0.49 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.8% over 3 years, 13.4% over 5 years and 7.5% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 5% of profits supports about 0.3% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 13.4% a year over five years.
Analysts expect 15.9% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 75%.
It returns 4.0% a year to shareholders (3.3% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has grown 6.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 42 consecutive years, raising it 10.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 19,744 employees, each generates about $535K of revenue, 1.5x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 5.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $78K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.3M (8x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
